architecture.approach: Three credential paths share one rule: the secret never travels and is never stored in a readable form. OIDC stays a pure module (server/src/utils/oidc.ts) with an injectable fetch, so the whole verification logic is unit tested against a fake provider without network access (CON-109). Two-factor keeps the cryptography in server/src/utils/totp.ts (Node crypto, no dependency), the encryption in server/src/utils/secretBox.ts (AES-256-GCM, HKDF, AAD = user id, CON-112) and the state machine in server/src/utils/twoFactor.ts, which is the only module that challenges, verifies and locks. API tokens are digests plus scopes from the day they are created, so a leaked database is useless without the server key. The controllers stay thin: they validate with express-validator, call the utility, and answer with fixed codes that the client maps to language.

dataModel.flowDescription: Single sign-on: /start loads the discovery document, creates a PKCE verifier, a state and a nonce, writes an SsoState row holding only the state hash with a ten-minute expiry, and redirects the browser to the provider. The provider returns to /callback, which deletes the state row (single use), exchanges the code with the verifier, verifies the ID token, and resolves the account: an already linked (provider, subject) wins, otherwise the provider-verified email links or creates the account with a random unknown password and ssoOnly true. A session is either issued directly and handed over in the URL fragment of /sso/complete, or, when two-factor is on, replaced by a challenge in the fragment of the login page. Two-factor sign-in: the password step writes a TwoFactorChallenge row (hashed nonce, five minutes, TTL) and returns a signed challenge; the second step verifies the authenticator code or a recovery code with conditional writes so a code or a code hash is consumed exactly once, then issues the session. Token creation: the plain token is returned once while the ApiToken row keeps the digest, the display prefix, the scopes, the workspace and the expiry; using the token resolves the row by digest, checks workspace and scopes on top of the owner's role, and revokes or expires it by looking at revokedAt and expiresAt on every request.

securityConsiderations.description: Account endpoints live behind protect and rejectApiToken, so a personal API token gets 403 on /api/profile/2fa and /api/profile/sso; authenticateApiToken additionally refuses a token when the request has no workspace slug, which keeps tokens out of every account and workspace-management route (CON-511).

Only reversible-when-needed secrets are encrypted, and they are encrypted with authenticated encryption: AES-256-GCM with an HKDF-SHA256 key and the user id as AAD, so a ciphertext from another account fails to decrypt. Everything that only needs verification is a digest: SHA-256 for SSO state and challenge nonces, bcrypt for recovery codes, keyed PBKDF2-SHA256 for API tokens (CON-112).

The password step, the second step and the two-factor account routes sit behind the sensitive limiter (20 per 15 minutes per IP, GET exempt so a page can load). Above that, a challenge allows five wrong codes, and five consecutive failures across challenges set twoFactor.lockedUntil for fifteen minutes (CON-514).

SSO failures log only the error name and message and the browser always receives one of the fixed SsoErrorCode values; the user schema marks every two-factor secret and hash as select: false and the toJSON transform reduces twoFactor to { enabled, enabledAt }; token listing projects an explicit field set that excludes tokenHash (CON-501, CON-517).

totp.test.ts verifies the RFC vectors, the window and the replay guard; secretBox.test.ts verifies tamper and cross-context failure; apiTokens.test.ts verifies the format, digests and scope subsetting; oidc.test.ts and ssoRedirect.test.ts cover verification and redirect safety; the integration suites drive the SSO, two-factor and token flows end to end (CON-402, CON-404).

performanceConsiderations.strategy: Token digests use PBKDF2 with 10,000 iterations: a few milliseconds per authenticated request, while a leaked digest stays expensive to attack offline. Generating a token is a single digest computation at creation time.

Challenge rows carry a TTL index and are replaced on every new sign-in (deleteMany per user), so the collection stays at roughly one row per account mid-sign-in; SSO state rows expire after ten minutes by the same mechanism.

Discovery and JWKS documents are cached for an hour, and an unknown kid triggers at most one refetch per minute, so token verification normally costs one cached crypto verification instead of an HTTP round trip.
authenticateApiToken writes lastUsedAt at most once a minute per token, so a busy script does not turn every read into a write.

risks.description: An SSO identity is used to take over an account whose email was never proved
risks.mitigation: A provider-verified email is required; an unverified account is taken over explicitly (password, tokens and sessions dropped) and a second identity of the same provider is refused as account_conflict

risks.description: Rotating JWT_SECRET or losing TWO_FACTOR_KEY makes stored TOTP secrets unreadable
risks.mitigation: A dedicated TWO_FACTOR_KEY keeps rotations independent, both are validated at boot, and a failed decryption is treated as a missing factor rather than a success

risks.description: A leaked API token is used for automation beyond its intent
risks.mitigation: One workspace, scopes limited to the owner's permissions, refusal on account routes, ten tokens maximum, optional expiry, immediate revocation and digest-only storage

risks.description: Provider metadata changes break SSO verification
risks.mitigation: Discovery/JWKS caching with a bounded refetch, explicit claim checks and fixed browser error codes instead of stack traces
